title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting al-Shabab
description: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.Uganda's acting army spokesperson
body: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time. He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces."As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security". The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries. The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence. In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside  about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements. Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns. They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support. A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

schema.headline: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of fighting al-Shabab

title: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
description: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.In a ma
body: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer. "We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said."They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.The company said it shared Australia's goal of protecting young people online "but there are better and more effective ways" than a ban."As we challenge this law in court, we'll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures," said Reddit's chief communications officer Adam Collins.Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats." "We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November. Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.

schema.headline: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court

title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
description: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the f
body: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC MonitoringFighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition."The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping"."It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday. And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday."I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV."I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month. If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

schema.headline: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire

title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
description: Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.Nearly 3,000
body: Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions. Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops." Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

schema.headline: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace

title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
description: Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in GermanyByJames ChaterRioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturda
body: Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in GermanyByJames ChaterRioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police detain a demonstrator dressed as Batman in FrankfurtOn Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended."We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.Image source, ReutersImage caption, People try to break through a window of a Frankfurt shop selling weaponsSimilar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations. In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind". A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe. In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.Figure caption, Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across EuropeFrench Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported, external that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

schema.headline: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent

title: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime
description: Warning: Distressing content and strong languageSamira says she never used to be political."I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BB
body: Warning: Distressing content and strong languageSamira says she never used to be political."I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BBC Panorama.But that all changed the day her only child was shot dead in front of her by Iranian security forces. Sixteen-year-old Sevda was taking part in protests against Iran's repressive regime that engulfed the country earlier this year - before the US and Israel launched widespread air strikes which killed the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.Samira's grief became fury as Iran's authorities then hindered, rather than helped, her search for her daughter's body, she says."I realised that finding Sevda wasn't the end, but just the beginning of all the harassment they put me through."Samira made a dramatic escape from Iran on foot, navigating dangerous mountainous terrain.She now lives abroad in hiding, describing herself as a "one-woman army fighting the regime". In a search for accountability and justice after her daughter's death, she is intent on naming the members of the security forces and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the protests."They'll bring me to the brink of death before they kill me, but finding me won't be easy… Return to normal life? There is no going back," she says.Samira is among several Iranians the BBC has spoken to since the start of the year. Some, still inside the country, told Panorama they wanted to speak out despite the risks, saying they had found it difficult to hold on to hope once the mass protests had been brutally crushed.The Iranian embassy in London told Panorama that peaceful and legitimate protests had been hijacked by foreign powers, including the US, which promoted violence, provided weapons and equipment, and compromised public security.Sevda was killed on 9 January as she and Samira took part in huge demonstrations on the outskirts of the capital Tehran which had begun the previous month. They had been sparked by economic discontent, before escalating into calls for an end to the country's Islamic Republic.Though Samira denies she was especially political then, she says her daughter was. Sevda's idols were two other young women - Mahsa Amini, whose death in custody after an alleged violation against the mandatory headscarf triggered mass protests, and Nika Shakarami, who was killed during a subsequent uprising against Iran's strict Islamic dress code for women."She kept them alive in her thoughts and always wanted to continue their path [of resistance]," Samira says.The day before Sevda was killed, the numbers protesting had been particularly high. Samira says she and Sevda had responded to a call by Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah (king), for demonstrations. "The security forces had lost control," she says.The swell in numbers had spooked Iran's government, and the following day a shoot-to-kill order was announced, Samira says. But she had thought it just an empty threat."They lied so much in Iran… We couldn't imagine a massacre of that scale."And they were reassured, she says, by US President Trump's promise that he had their backs.He had told US media on 8 January: "I have let [the Iranian authorities] know that if they start killing people, which they tend to do during their riots… we're going to hit them very hard."But nevertheless the crowds appeared smaller on the 9th, Samira says. Sevda seemed to know the risks, she says. Her daughter took off her earrings and gave them to her grandmother. She also shared her phone passcode with Samira.The mother and daughter gathered with the rest of the protesters. Sevda then stood on a dustbin and began leading a chant."It seemed there were more forces than people," Samira says of the area where they were. "I don't know how, within one day, they gathered so many… Basijis and IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] forces."The IRGC defends the country's Islamic establishment, and the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force are volunteers for the IRGC."A sniper fired from the roof of a building on our right. The bullet must have come from the rooftop. The bullet went through her heart. I couldn't even scream. I just stared at Sevda - her body lying lifeless. Blood was gushing out her mouth and nose. I couldn't believe it, I couldn't believe she was dying. Her eyes were still looking at me."Samira says she managed to get Sevda to hospital and she was told they were operating on her, but then the door opened and she saw Sevda had been zipped into a body bag.Sevda's body was taken away. Samira says it took her days to find her daughter again. Like many others, she found herself at one of Tehran's largest morgues."Teenagers - young boys and girls. So many had been killed," she cries."I died with every bag I unzipped. I'd never seen so many bodies. But I wouldn't give up."She finally found her daughter. "Three bodies were piled on top of Sevda. That's how we found her."Iranian authorities acknowledge that more than 3,000 people were killed in the protests, but claim some were members of the security forces. One human rights group, Hrana, however, estimates the number of dead stands at more than 7,000, most of them protesters. Finding Sevda's body was just the beginning of Samira's battle with the authorities, she says.To be allowed to take away the body for burial, she says she was forced to say that "terrorists" rather than the security forces had been responsible for Sevda's death."They did this to cover up what they'd done on 8 and 9 January, to hide how many people they had killed. They silenced families by telling them to say their loved ones were killed by Israeli or American terrorists."Nevertheless she was barred from visiting the grave after the funeral, or organising a tombstone, she says.And Samira says the harassment continued. A few days before the ceremony to mark 40 days since Sevda died - highly significant in Iranian culture - she says she was summoned by a local branch of the Ministry of Intelligence."They told me: 'You should give us an interview and say that Sevda was a Basiji and she was killed by the protesters. Then we will announce her [as] a martyr - you will then receive perks, a house, or anything that you want.'"She is sure this offer was prompted by fear, because she had shared Sevda's death with an Iranian media organisation based in London, once the internet had been reconnected in the country."It scared them that I was in touch with external networks or those outside Iran."To avoid giving the interview, Samira fled Iran as soon as the 40th day anniversary was over."I didn't want to trade with my child's blood."She says people smugglers helped her to escape. She crossed rivers and mountains to get to safety.A video she made of herself fleeing makes clear her fury."This crap government, these bastards, they've harassed me so much," she tells the camera as she marches along a mountain path bordered by a deep ravine.Samira says after she continued to give interviews to foreign media from abroad, she was charged in absentia with a string of offences, including "moharebeh" - waging war against God - which can carry the death penalty.To mark what would have been Sevda's 17th birthday, her relatives and friends held a vigil - with Samira watching from exile on a livestream."Then suddenly, the feed cut out," she says.She discovered that the event had been raided, she says, and some of her family and friends arrested by the IRGC.She says her family was warned by the authorities that, if they continued to gather at Sevda's grave, her body would be exhumed and moved elsewhere.Now, Samira shares the names, online, of Iranian security force members and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the 8 and 9 January protests she and Sevda joined."I want justice to be served for every single person whose name I expose, because they have killed so many young people. My goal is for them to be identified so they can be put on trial," she says.When one of the men Samira named online was later found dead, a regime supporter offered a $5,000 (£3,732) reward for information about her whereabouts, presuming she was responsible. Iranian state media has since reported the arrest of nine people in connection with the death.Despite the risks, Samira says she refuses to be silenced."Every day and every second without Sevda is very difficult for me. It's like a mother who has lost her heart, who has lost her being, has lost her life…"But the fact that Sevda is not breathing has made it possible for me to stand on my feet… to think about honouring her life and her path... all those bodies I saw, all those body bags I opened looking for Sevda, they all made me fight the Islamic Republic until my last breath."

schema.headline: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime

title: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
description: The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.Carried by winds to nearby Singapore
body: The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia."People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders."There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan."Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess."The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added."The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires."It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours."Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania."The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side."As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh. "The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

schema.headline: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache

title: Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
description: It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbul
body: It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence."We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash but that determining its probable cause will be a "lengthy investigatory process".Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time. Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the safety board.Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit appears to be "we're out of time".The seven people killed who were travelling as passengers were identified in a joint statement from their families as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma and Charlie - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot. As well as those killed, one man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the plane nosedived onto the street.

schema.headline: Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
description: Image source, Getty ImagesBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesThe US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administrati
body: Image source, Getty ImagesBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesThe US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count. The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state. Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate. The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term. The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction. "The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots. California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible. Figure caption, What are Americans voting for this election?The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch". With additional reporting by the BBC's David Willis

schema.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes

title: Russian bombing kills 26 people at humanitarian aid centre in Ukraine, Kyiv says
description: Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble". He said
body: Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble". He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, next week, US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff said on X.Since the talks were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.No major breakthrough is expected at the talks. Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace".Witkoff said US negotiators would also meet European and Nato officials this week in Brussels.

title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
description: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian dr
body: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note – a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts."The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us.""But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.  Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings."My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up.""Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app. Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches."This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident."All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said."It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

schema.headline: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine

title: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise
description: Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of vote
body: Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.Organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, the protest drew many of the alliance's most prominent leaders in a show of strength against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.Protesters waved flags and chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power".It was the latest in a series of protests over electoral roll revision that the opposition says has removed eligible voters to benefit the Bharatiya Janata Party. The BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.The crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi known for hosting major political and cultural events. Some protesters sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs, while others waited beneath a large canopy in the colours of the Indian flag to hear opposition leaders speak.Gandhi and several senior opposition leaders arrived at the venue in an open jeep, travelling through crowds of cheering supporters.The event was also attended by Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, alongside leaders of regional parties such as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Supriya Sule and Tejashwi Yadav.Addressing the crowds, Rahul Gandhi said those gathered had sent a message to Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar."This is not the voice of a single political party or of politicians. It is the voice of India's youth, women, farmers and workers," he said."We will not allow democracy to be destroyed in India. We will not allow the constitution to be destroyed."Other opposition leaders echoed Gandhi's criticism of the Election Commission. Congress president Kharge said the alliance would continue its campaign until Kumar resigned, while Banerjee pledged to keep fighting against what she described as threats to democracy.Speaking to reporters in Delhi on Sunday, senior BJP leader and federal minister JP Nadda accused the opposition of trying to create unrest and destabilise the government under the guise of defending democracy.He described the rally as a "calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy - in the name of democracy".At the centre of the dispute is an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which has resulted in more than 130 million names being removed from India's draft electoral rolls.The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate registrations and the names of people who have died, moved away or are otherwise ineligible to vote. It says eligible voters who have been wrongly excluded can seek to have their names restored.But opposition parties allege that the process is removing legitimate voters and could benefit the governing BJP in future elections.The controversy deepened in September when The Indian Express newspaper reported, external that Kumar had made key decisions about the revision despite repeated objections from the two other election commissioners.The poll panel said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.Sunday's rally followed weeks of protests over the voter-list revision, including demonstrations by student groups and the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). Last month, Gandhi led tens of thousands on a march from central Delhi's Connaught Place to the Supreme Court, demanding Kumar's resignation.The CJP also backed Sunday's rally but chose not to participate. Its founder Abhijeet Dipke said the group wanted to maintain its independence from established political parties.The event took place under strict conditions imposed by Delhi Police. According to local media reports, organisers were required to end the gathering by 5pm, install CCTV cameras at the venue and ensure that protesters did not march beyond the designated grounds.The restrictions came against a backdrop of tensions over the policing of demonstrations in the capital. On 10 October, several leaders of the CJP were detained during protests against Kumar, while BBC reporters witnessed police dragging demonstrators away and beating some with batons.At Ramlila Maidan, however, the atmosphere was largely peaceful, with people of different ages and professions turning out to express their concerns about the integrity of India's elections."We don't even know if this is a people's mandate or a stolen mandate," Isha, a development sector professional from Delhi, told the BBC.Deepro Guha, a lawyer from Delhi, said he was concerned about the way the revision had been carried out."It's important because voting is the basis of democracy. If people's names are removed without any explanation, there is a problem," he said.

schema.headline: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise

title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
description: Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and
body: Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely."The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce. The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit. A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network"."ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores. The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.Additional reporting by Shiona McCallumHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story? title: US midterms campaign set to be most expensive ever recorded
description: The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record
body: The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle."Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.

schema.headline: US midterms campaign set to be most expensive ever recorded

title: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash
description: An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.D
body: An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people. The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and  was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself."Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB". Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death."Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said."Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit. "Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post, external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.More than 540 people were on board both trains.

schema.headline: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash
